title: One-to-one counting
keyIdea: Every object gets exactly one number word.

kid: When you count things, each thing gets exactly one number. Point to each object once and say one number for it.
Don't skip any, and don't count any twice. A good trick is to slide each thing into a 'done' pile as you count it.
adult: One-to-one correspondence means pairing each object with exactly one number word, said in order. It is the first rule of reliable counting.

The usual slips are counting an object twice, skipping one, or saying the words faster than pointing. Touching or moving each item fixes most of them. The same pairing idea comes back later, for example when matching items between two sets to compare their sizes.

familyTip: Count stairs, socks or grapes together, touching each one. Make a deliberate mistake now and then and let your child catch you.

practice.prompt: Sam counts 5 apples but touches one apple twice. What number does Sam say at the end?
practice.hint: Each touch gets a number word. One apple got two words.
practice.explain: Five apples plus one extra touch gives six number words, so Sam says 6, one too many.

practice.prompt: Count the stars: ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★. How many are there?
practice.hint: Point at each star once as you say a number.

practice.prompt: Which way of counting blocks is most reliable?
choices: Point at each block once while saying one number
Say the numbers quickly while looking at the pile
Count the big blocks, then guess the rest
practice.hint: Think about which way makes sure every block gets one number.
practice.explain: Pointing at each block once, with one number each, pairs every block with exactly one number word.

practice.prompt: Put the counting words in order.
practice.explain: Counting words always come in the same order: one, two, three, four, five.

pool.hint: Slide your finger along and count each heart once.

pool.prompt: Mia counts cups and says 'one, two, three, four', but she missed one cup without giving it a number. How many cups are there really?
pool.hint: The missed cup still needs a number.
pool.explain: Four cups got numbers and one was missed, so there are 5 cups.

pool.prompt: Ravi points to 3 pencils but says 'one, two, three, four'. What went wrong?
choices: He said one more number than the pencils he pointed to
He pointed at too many pencils
pool.hint: Compare the number of words with the number of pencils.
pool.explain: He said four words for three pencils, so his words and his pointing did not match one-to-one.

pool.prompt: Leo touches each of {n} toy cars once and says one number for each. What number does he say last?
pool.explain: He says {n}: one number for each of the {n} cars.

pool.prompt: Zara counts {n} beads but touches one bead twice. What number does she say at the end?
pool.hint: The bead touched twice got two numbers.
pool.explain: {n} beads plus one extra touch gives {=n+1} number words, one too many.

pool.prompt: Omar counts {n} spoons but skips one by mistake. What number does he say last?
pool.hint: The skipped spoon got no number.
pool.explain: He gives numbers to only {=n-1} of the {n} spoons, so he says {=n-1}.

pool.prompt: What is the best way to make sure you don't count a sock twice?
choices: Move each sock to a new pile as you count it
Count as fast as you can
Only count the socks you can see from far away
pool.hint: How can you tell which socks are already counted?
pool.explain: Moving each counted sock to a new pile means it can't be counted again.
